My Journey & Philosophy

From the countryside of Homabay to medical training, literature, and social reform.

I am Wanga Domnic Okoth, a second born in a family of three raised in Rangwe Constituency, West Gem Ward, Homabay County, in the Kenyan countryside away from the shores of Lake Victoria. Growing in the countryside never limited the horizons I imagined for myself or the opportunities I believed life could offer. Graced to be raised by parents who believed in me, encouraged curiosity and open mindedness, promoted ingenuity and shaped my worldview in ways that continue to influence how I interact with people, society and the world.

My learning began long before I started schooling but first stepped into a classroom at Heartspring Junior Academy where I undertook my primary education, before proceeding to Kabianga School for my secondary education. I am currently pursuing my medical studies at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT) where through meeting humanity at its rawest form I have come to realise and of the strong opinion that healthcare must extend beyond diagnosis and treatment of disease to recognising the dignity, experiences and humanity of the individual whose worldview has been shaken by the ailment.

As an essential part of medicine I'm strongly committed to mental health, an area in which I am actively involved through the Healed Healers Community Based Organisation. I am particularly interested in the intersection of human wellbeing, psychological health and the broader social conditions that shape our lives.

Literature occupies a very important place in my life. I have always been drawn to stories and their abilities to articulate experiences that would otherwise remain unspoken. I believe that through literature human beings find their purest voices and through relatable stories we learn to identify and interact with each not as strangers but as those connected to us through similar experiences. Through literature I explore the human conditioning, question society and look for meaning in questions that do not always have easy answers in a complex world.

Literature

What Unites People?

Presidents? Flags? Constitution? Armies? No. Stories.

Yes, stories. Nothing can rival the power of a well told story. No enemy can defeat it and no great ruler can afford to ignore it. We may disagree about almost everything, but a story can make us pause long enough to understand why another person thinks, feels, acts or loves the way they do. Stories give us a sense of belonging to one another, allowing us to recognise ourselves as members of the human race even as we inhabit different civilisations.

Storytelling is an antidote to numbness and apathy. Through shared stories we reconnect and learn to care about each other’s sorrows, troubles and triumphs. As we journey into another person’s story we realise just how much they resemble the people we know, and perhaps ourselves. Their stories read in many ways like our own. Through literature we live different lives at the same time, and we learn to connect even with lives lived centuries before us.

Literature, particularly through fiction, gives a voice to thoughts and feelings we have not yet learnt to articulate to one another comfortably. In it the abandoned lover expresses their deepest feelings that reason alone can’t quantify, the oppressed find a language through which to give voice to their suffering, and the cancer survivor finds a way to walk others through their near-death experience. The forgotten, the misunderstood and the rebellious find somewhere to speak and perhaps to be heard. From the pages of a book, a nihilist tries to get meaning from a rather indifferent world.

Through literature, humanity finds its purest voices.

Book One

Dare Dream

What happens when a child dares to imagine a different future in an environment where even tomorrow isn’t guaranteed?

Dare Dream is a fictional narrative centred on a boy, Brian, raised in the slums of Kariadudu. His parents had moved there after being failed by the system that promised jobs and opportunities but delivered hopelessness and took away dignity. Despite the circumstances around him, Brian is raised with a different understanding of possibilities and success.

The boy observes what goes on around him: corruption carried out by a failed system, injustice to the voiceless, extortion of the have-nots by the haves of the land, and irresponsibility of individuals in nation building. His parents instill in him a different blueprint, a system of abundance wired into his brain. In an area filled with hopelessness, corruption, exploitation of the poor and no prospects of livelihoods changing, the young boy dares to dream of a better tomorrow, even when tomorrow itself isn’t guaranteed.

The family relocates to their rural home, where Brian begins his schooling at nine years old in his quest to become a doctor. His journey eventually takes him to high school, where the unfamiliar social environment presents new challenges. Faced with culture shock and the difficulty of belonging, he turns to solitude as his biggest weapon. It is within this solitude that he makes what he considers one of life’s greatest discoveries: himself.

At its heart, Dare Dream is an exploration of ambition, the influence of family in becoming, social inequality, self-discovery and the human capacity to imagine and experience change.

Book Two

Beyond the White Coat

What happens when the pursuit of a childhood dream brings you face to face with questions that you have never taken interest in and worse still to which humanity has not given any credible answers?

Beyond the White Coat is a story about a young boy, Brian, who joins university to pursue his long-held dream of becoming a doctor. The university introduces him to a world quite different from the one he had imagined. The boy experiences a culture shock, not just in the city but also along the corridors of the university, where what used to be talked about in whispers from his origins is now practiced publicly without any restraint.

He walks the journey through med school, and his willpower to remain is tested by unforgiving instructors, the emotional demands of medical training and the heavy pressure of the programme. Yes, he persists. In those laboratories filled with formaldehyde, clinical encounters and the demanding corridors of medicine, arise questions older than his ancestors: questions about mortality and what humans truly understand about death; questions about faith, morality and the evolution of moral values in society; questions about what makes an action right or wrong, and whether the explanations we have inherited are sufficient to guide our human experiences.

Beyond the White Coat explores the tension between scientific knowledge and existentialism. It considers the limitations of human understanding and the deeper questions that emerge when the pursuit of medicine becomes an encounter with love, life, faith, death and the complexity of being human.

Convictions & Advocacy

Pan-Africanist philosophy, institutional reform, and confronting uncomfortable truths.

Pan-Africanist Vision

A Pan Africanist at heart I believe deeply in the restoration of Africans dignity as humans who can contribute to global intellectual conversations and not as subhumans to be conquered. The historical and continued alienation of African people and global systems that have sustained inequality continue to be issues of great importance when it comes to my understanding of the world.

I hold the conviction that Africa's transformation is possible through selfless and servanthood leadership, as it was in our culture before colonisation, accountable institutions, sound policies and systems and a people willing to question the realities that shape its societies.

Fearless Truth & Education

I'm of the view that a society can never change unless the reality is confronted and I believe the time is right that we learn to tell ourselves hard uncomfortable truths and ask the difficult questions especially the ones that we have learnt to avoid over the years.

Ultimately I am of great interest in questions that connect medicine, mental health, literature, African history and current affairs, society and humanity. Education to me is not merely a means of personal development but an opportunity to acquire knowledge, perspective and capacity to meaningfully engage with and contribute to the world around me.
